conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve had this sharp belly pain for about a day. It’s all over, and I’ve thrown up twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or blood in your vomit or stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fevers. And nothing bloody. But I haven’t been able to keep food or my medicines down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also noticed you were a bit confused when you arrived. Are you feeling more clear now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little. I was really out of it earlier. My daughter said I couldn’t remember where I was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with your liver condition. We call it hepatic encephalopathy. We’ve given you lactulose to help clear your mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I take that at home. But I couldn’t keep it down yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Not taking it can make the confusion worse. We’re giving it more frequently now to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Is the belly pain from my liver too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. We did a CT scan of your abdomen. It showed some narrowing in parts of your colon, which could mean mild inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation? Like an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re treating it like a possible gut infection for now. But your stool tests didn’t show C. diff or other common bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be viral, or related to your liver disease. One blood culture showed a bacteria called Corynebacterium, but we think it’s a contaminant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. You don’t have a fever or signs of a bloodstream infection. We’ve stopped IV antibiotics and will send you home with a short course of cipro by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. What about my liver? The scan said something about a lesion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan showed your liver looks nodular, which is expected with cirrhosis. There’s a spot we can’t fully rule out, so we recommend a follow-up MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Could it be cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say for sure, but it could just be regenerative nodules. The MRI will help clarify. Your MELD score is 15, which means your liver function is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do the MRI. What about my other meds? I take a lot for depression and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your sedating meds like trazodone and seroquel while you were confused. Now that you’re more alert, we’re restarting them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But you said not to take them if I’m confused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. If you feel overly drowsy or confused at home, skip those and call your psychiatrist. They can worsen encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain is gone, and I’m thinking more clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your lactate level, which was high, has come down. That means your body is handling stress better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is still low, but stable. Platelets are low too, which is common in cirrhosis. We stopped your heparin shot just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Your hemoglobin is stable. The slight drop was likely from dehydration. We’ll check your platelets at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the cipro for 4 more days. Take your lactulose, rifaximin, and omeprazole regularly. Watch for confusion or belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep checking your blood sugar. We’ll continue your sliding scale insulin as needed. Your glucose was 94 this morning—perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the varices? My last scope showed small ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since they were grade 1 and not bleeding, we don’t need to start beta-blockers now, but it’s something to discuss with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if symptoms return. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re discharging you with home services to help for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. My daughter will be relieved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: She’s listed as your contact. We’ll make sure she gets the instructions too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want her to know what to watch for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Confusion, severe pain, or vomiting are reasons to call or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up with your follow-ups, especially the MRI and blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel free to call if anything comes up. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and get well soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You’re in the hospital because your daughter brought you in due to confusion and trouble standing. Do you remember coming in last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was sleepy. My daughter said I wasn’t making sense. I just felt off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You were drowsy and a bit confused when you arrived. We’re trying to figure out what caused it. You have cirrhosis from hepatitis C and alcohol use, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had that for years. And I’ve been drinking… not every day, but most days, a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your daughter mentioned you hadn’t been taking your lactulose regularly. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like it. It makes me nauseous. Sometimes I throw it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of why you were confused. Lactulose helps clear toxins from your body when your liver isn’t working well. Not taking it can lead to mental changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know it was that important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It really is. We also noticed you’ve been taking more of your psychiatric medicines than prescribed. Your daughter said your new Wellbutrin was gone early, and some Seroquel pills are missing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was supposed to take Wellbutrin twice a day. No one told me it was once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely contribute to confusion. Taking too much of certain medications, especially with liver disease, can build up in your system and affect your brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean to. I just wanted to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why we’ve paused most of your psychiatric meds for now. We consulted psychiatry, and they recommend restarting only Wellbutrin and trazodone at lower doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the others? Seroquel, nortriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping those for now. They can worsen confusion, especially when combined. Your psychiatrist will help decide if they’re needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you extra lactulose in the ER to help clear your system. Your CT scans of the head and abdomen were okay—no bleeding or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection? I’ve been nauseous for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine and blood cultures showed no growth, so no active infection. The nausea may be from your medications or liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my liver? Is it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows your liver is still cirrhotic with portal hypertension, but no new tumors or blockages. Your MELD score is 15, which means moderate liver dysfunction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my drinking? I had a beer the day before I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could have triggered withdrawal symptoms—your high blood pressure and fast heart rate when you arrived suggest that. We’re monitoring you with a scale called CIWA and gave you Ativan to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I was in withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common. We’ve started you on thiamine, folic acid, B12, and a multivitamin to support your body, especially since you’ve been drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re new. They help prevent complications from alcohol use, like nerve damage or anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your platelets and white blood cells are low, but that’s been your baseline. No signs of bleeding or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cirrhosis can suppress bone marrow function. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It was high last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s coming down. We gave you hydralazine once, but now it’s stable. Likely due to withdrawal and stress. We’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? More alert?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I feel like my head is clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your mental status is improving. We’re going to keep you on lactulose three times a day and restart your diabetes meds. Can you eat something light?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. Maybe some broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and advance as you tolerate. Your daughter mentioned you were in a relapse program but got discharged. Do you want help getting back into one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do… I keep trying to quit, but I need more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work is going to help you look into the Geriatric Day Program. It might be a better fit for your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. The tremors and mild asterixis we saw early on are improving. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You need to follow up with your psychiatrist and liver doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with my psychiatrist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. They’ll call if they can see you sooner. And a nurse will come to your home to review your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. Your mental status is clear, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ve learned I need to take my lactulose, even if I don’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And take only the meds we’ve prescribed—no extra doses. Your liver can’t process too many medicines at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise. And I’ll try to stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do for your health. We’re here to support you. You’re going home with services, so someone will check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge instructions are ready. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if I feel confused again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor right away. It could mean your liver is struggling or you’re not taking your meds. And if it’s severe, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and keep those follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve had this really bad pain in my right upper belly for about a day now. It’s constant and sharp. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Any fever, diarrhea, or blood in your stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or diarrhea. I haven’t noticed blood, but I’ve been so sick I might’ve missed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We ran some tests in the ER. Your labs show low white blood cells and platelets, which we expect with your liver disease. Your liver enzymes are elevated, especially AST.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my liver’s been bad for years. Cirrhosis from hepatitis and drinking. But I haven’t had a drink in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We checked your alcohol level and it was negative. We’re concerned about possible infection or inflammation in your gut. A CT scan showed colitis in the right side of your colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Colitis? But I haven’t had diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes colitis can cause pain and vomiting before diarrhea starts. We’re watching for that. We also saw slow blood flow in part of your portal vein, but no clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Is my liver getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cirrhosis is still there, but no new damage we can see. The slow flow may be from your portal hypertension, which we already knew about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I feel really tired and kind of out of it. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You were given morphine in the ER. But we’re also watching for hepatic encephalopathy, given your history. We’ll keep you on lactulose and rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I take those at home. And I’ve been on spironolactone for fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held the spironolactone for now because your blood pressure was low and you’ve been vomiting—didn’t want to dehydrate you more. We’ll restart it when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My heart’s racing too. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate is in the 100s, which we think is from dehydration due to vomiting and not eating. We’re giving IV fluids. We also started you on a protocol to watch for alcohol withdrawal, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not having withdrawal. I haven’t had a drink in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know, but with your history, we monitor closely. You scored low on the scale, so we’re just giving Ativan if needed. You’re not showing signs of withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pain, but less than yesterday. I threw up once last night, and I had loose stools this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps confirm our suspicion of gastroenteritis—likely an infection in your gut. We sent stool tests to rule out serious infections like C. diff or Salmonella.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my liver acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not primarily. Your liver numbers are a bit high, but not enough to suggest alcoholic hepatitis. Your MELD score is stable. The pain and vomiting are more likely from the colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the blood test that showed low white cells?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have chronic leukopenia from your liver disease. This admission, it’s a bit lower, possibly due to the infection or fluid shifts. We’ll repeat it before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my platelets?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still low, but stable. That’s expected with cirrhosis. No signs of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m worried about the colitis. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed no complications like perforation or abscess. It’s likely a mild infectious colitis. We’re not giving antibiotics because your symptoms are improving and no dangerous bacteria were found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and other pathogens. That supports a viral or mild bacterial gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just something I have to ride out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your pain is better, you’re keeping fluids down, and your labs are trending up. We’re going to do a flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to check for hemorrhoids or polyps since you had a positive stool test before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have hemorrhoids. But I haven’t seen blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sigmoidoscopy is just to be safe, especially with your history of polyps. It’s a quick procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the sigmoidoscopy. The doctor said the colon looked normal. No inflammation or bleeding. They saw external hemorrhoids, but no polyps or active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Was it okay to not take my prep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since it was only to the sigmoid colon and you’ve had loose stools, it was fine. No need for biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your white count improved, and your kidney function is stable. Your mental clarity is much better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. Still tired, but not foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We restarted your spironolactone this morning. You’re also back on all your home meds, including lactulose and rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We used insulin while you were here to control sugars, but you’re not on it now. Just your usual oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back, or you have fever, vomiting, or bloody stools, call your doctor. Keep taking your lactulose and avoid alcohol and marijuana, which can worsen symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I should stop. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re referring you to hepatology and your psychiatrist to help. You’ll also get a follow-up CBC to check your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take oxycodone 5 mg every six hours if needed, but only for breakthrough pain. You have ten pills, no refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds are on your discharge list—rifaximin, lactulose, omeprazole, quetiapine, trazodone, vitamins. Take them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll try to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up with your doctors. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will go over your discharge papers, and you should be ready to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing—my mom died from cirrhosis. I’m scared that’ll happen to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re taking steps—no alcohol, staying on your meds, coming in when you’re sick. That makes a big difference. We’ll keep supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I ask about the chest X-ray? I saw it was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we did a chest X-ray to make sure you didn’t have pneumonia, especially with vomiting. It was clear—just some old scarring, no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling ready to go home. It’s been a long few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll make sure your home services are set up. Rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s better. But why am I so confused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate the taste… makes me bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it’s important. We’ve given you a dose already, and we’ll give it every two hours tonight to help clear your mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… will I feel better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
